clinicalPearls: The most severe form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, usually caused by variants in STAR encoding the steroidogenic acute regulatory protein.
StAR mediates transport of cholesterol into the mitochondrion, the rate-limiting first step of all steroid hormone synthesis.
The block impairs production of every class of adrenal and gonadal steroid: mineralocorticoids, glucocorticoids and sex steroids.
Cholesterol accumulates within steroidogenic cells, producing lipid-laden, enlarged adrenal glands that give the condition its name.
Affected infants typically present with severe salt-wasting adrenal crisis in the neonatal period.
46,XY infants have female-appearing external genitalia because testicular androgen synthesis fails in utero.
46,XX individuals have normal external genitalia at birth but develop ovarian failure, and cyclical ovarian steroidogenesis can cause later cyst formation.
A phenotypically milder, non-classic form with predominant glucocorticoid deficiency and later presentation is increasingly recognised.
reference.pathophysiology: Lipoid congenital adrenal hyperplasia is an autosomal recessive disorder that most often results from loss-of-function variants in STAR, the gene encoding the steroidogenic acute regulatory protein, and less commonly from severe variants in the cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme (CYP11A1). StAR shuttles cholesterol from the outer to the inner mitochondrial membrane, where side-chain cleavage converts it to pregnenolone; this is the obligatory first and rate-limiting step of all steroidogenesis. When StAR function is lost, the adrenal cortex and gonads cannot initiate hormone synthesis, so mineralocorticoids, glucocorticoids and sex steroids are all deficient. The disease is classically described as a two-hit process: an initial impairment of StAR-dependent steroidogenesis is compounded by progressive intracellular accumulation of cholesterol esters, which are toxic and physically disrupt the remaining StAR-independent steroidogenic capacity, leading to massively engorged, lipid-laden glands. Loss of cortisol feedback drives high corticotrophin, and loss of aldosterone causes salt wasting with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypovolaemia. In 46,XY fetuses the failure of testicular testosterone production prevents masculinisation, resulting in female-appearing genitalia, whereas 46,XX fetuses appear normal at birth because ovarian steroid synthesis is quiescent in fetal life; at expected puberty gonadotrophin-driven stimulation can transiently produce oestrogen and provoke ovarian cyst formation before the gonad also fails.
additionalDifferentials: Adrenoleukodystrophy and other causes of primary adrenal insufficiency in infancy
Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome in a 46,XY infant with female genitalia
additionalInvestigations: Serum electrolytes for hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia
Serum cortisol with a raised ACTH indicating primary adrenal failure
Plasma renin activity and aldosterone confirming mineralocorticoid deficiency
Broadly low adrenal and gonadal steroid profile across all pathways
Adrenal imaging that may show enlarged lipid-laden glands
Karyotype with pelvic and gonadal imaging
STAR and CYP11A1 molecular genetic testing
redFlags: Neonatal salt-wasting crisis with hypovolaemic shock, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia
Hyperpigmentation and failure to thrive from unrecognised adrenal insufficiency
46,XY infant with female-appearing genitalia and intra-abdominal testes carrying malignancy risk
Circulatory collapse or arrhythmia during intercurrent illness
Delayed puberty or ovarian cysts in a 46,XX adolescent with the condition
reference.prognosis: Untreated classic disease is fatal in infancy from adrenal crisis, but with early diagnosis, lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement, salt supplementation in infancy and sex-steroid replacement, survival into adulthood is expected. Fertility is severely limited, and prognosis depends on avoidance of adrenal crises, monitoring of intra-abdominal gonads in 46,XY individuals, and multidisciplinary care of the disorder of sex development.
pitfalls: Assuming a 46,XY infant with female genitalia is unaffected until a salt-wasting crisis develops.
Attributing neonatal collapse to sepsis alone and missing underlying primary adrenal failure.
Expecting a single elevated precursor as in other forms; here essentially all steroids are low.
Overlooking the milder non-classic form that presents later with glucocorticoid deficiency and preserved mineralocorticoid function.
Neglecting surveillance of intra-abdominal gonads and later ovarian cyst formation.

management: Lifelong glucocorticoid replacement with hydrocortisone to correct the profound cortisol deficiency
Mineralocorticoid replacement with fludrocortisone, together with sodium chloride supplementation in infancy, to manage salt-wasting

Emergency treatment of adrenal crisis with parenteral hydrocortisone, fluid resuscitation and correction of hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia, supported by sick-day dosing rules and an emergency steroid card
Sex-steroid replacement from the expected time of puberty, guided by karyotype, gonadal status and sex of rearing, noting 46,XY infants have female-appearing genitalia
Regular monitoring of growth, electrolytes, renin and pubertal development to titrate replacement
Multidisciplinary paediatric endocrine care with input on sex assignment and later fertility counselling
Genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance of the STAR (or CYP11A1) defect
